docs.description:
Endurance-A would land on a CLPS lander in central SPA, traverse out of SPA through the Poincaré and Schrödinger basins, collect a total of 100-kg of samples from 12 sites, and deliver those samples to Artemis astronauts at the south pole, who retrieve the samples and bring them to Earth.

This tour visits 11 of these sites and is available in both EQ and SP projections. The EQ projection (Global Map) covers all 11 sites whereas the SP projection (South Pole Map) encompasses only 5 of the 11 sites but without the distortion which occurs in polar regions of the Global Map. To change projections, use the icon in the bottom left of the screen.

The path and science stations used in this tour are available as individual data products that can be added to and viewed in the map, independently of the tour. Use the icon to open the data panel and search for "Endurance-A".

docs.description:
Lunar Trailblazer is a pioneering small satellite mission for lunar water and lunar geology. Its goal is to map the form, abundance, and distribution of water on the Moon to understand the lunar water cycle. Lunar Trailblazer’s data will provide key information for future lunar surface exploration by mapping water ice and geologic units at high spatial resolution important to robotic and human exploration. Trailblazer will simultaneously measure composition (water and mineralogy), temperature, and thermophysical properties from a 100±30 km lunar polar orbit.

Lunar Trailblazer carries two instruments to achieve its science objectives: the High-resolution Volatiles and Minerals Moon Mapper (HVM3) from NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL), and the Lunar Thermal Mapper (LTM) from the University of Oxford, contributed by the United Kingdom Space Agency (UKSA). When used in conjunction, these two instruments provide the ability to simultaneously identify the various forms of water on the Moon, mineralogy, and temperature.

The HVM3 instrument is a pushbroom short-wave infrared imaging spectrometer based on the design of the Moon Mineralogy Mapper (M3) instrument previously flown on the Chandraayan-1 probe. M3 advanced our understanding of lunar mineralogy and was one of the first instruments to detect signs of hydration (water and hydroxyl) in sunlit regions of the Moon. HVM3 will build upon and extend M3’s legacy by extending the range of wavelengths over which data will be collected to determine the form of water and by using its enhanced sensitivity for measuring water ice in permanently shadowed regions of the Moon.

The LTM instrument will gather mid-wave infrared data to derive mineralogical composition and measure lunar surface temperatures. Measuring water and temperature at the same time will lead to improved understanding of factors that control the distribution of water. Lunar Trailblazer will be launched as a rideshare payload on Intuitive Machines’ second lunar lander (IM-2) launch.

This tour visits 8 sites of interest and is available in all 3 projections - EQ, SP, and NP. The EQ projection (Global Map) covers all 8 sites whereas the SP projection (South Pole Map) encompasses only 3 of the 8 sites and the NP projection (North Pole Map) only 1 site. However, the polar projections offer views of the data without the distortion which occurs in polar regions of the Global Map. To change projections, use the icon in the bottom left of the screen.

docs.description:
On August 19, 2022, NASA announced 13 candidate landing regions near the lunar South Pole as it continued preparations to send astronauts in a new generation of explorations of the Moon as part of the Artemis missions. Each region contains multiple potential landing sites for Artemis III, which will be the first of the Artemis missions to bring crew to the lunar surface, including the first woman to set foot on the Moon. Each of these regions is located within six degrees of latitude of the lunar South Pole. These areas were selected based upon a variety of factors including proximity to key geologic features (particularly permanently shadowed regions often found in near-polar craters), slope and smoothness of terrain enabling safe landing, lighting conditions, and windows for communication with Earth.

The 13 regions identified are:

  • Faustini Rim A
  • Peak Near Shackleton
  • Connecting Ridge
  • Connecting Ridge Extension
  • de Gerlache Rim 1
  • de Gerlache-Kocher Massif
  • Haworth
  • Malapert Massif
  • Mons Mouton Plateau
  • Nobile Rim 1
  • Nobile Rim 2
  • Amundsen Rim
docs.title: The Artemis Regions
Artemis III Candidate Landing Regions, S Pole
docs.description:
This layer depicts the 13 candidate landing regions for Artemis III announced by NASA on August 19 2022. Each region contains multiple potential landing sites for Artemis III, which will be the first of the Artemis missions to bring crew to the lunar surface, including the first woman to set foot on the Moon.

Each of these regions is located within six degrees of latitude of the lunar South Pole and, collectively, contain diverse geologic features. Together, the regions provide landing options for all potential Artemis III launch opportunities. Specific landing sites are tightly coupled to the timing of the launch window, so multiple regions ensure flexibility to launch throughout the year.

To select the regions, an agencywide team of scientists and engineers assessed the area near the lunar South Pole using data from NASA’s Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter and decades of publications and lunar science findings. In addition to considering launch window availability, the team evaluated regions based on their ability to accommodate a safe landing, using criteria including terrain slope, ease of communications with Earth, and lighting conditions. To determine accessibility, the team also considered combined capabilities of the Space Launch System rocket, the Orion spacecraft, and the SpaceX-provided Starship human landing system.

All regions considered are scientifically significant because of their proximity to the lunar South Pole, which is an area that contains permanently shadowed regions rich in resources and in terrain unexplored by humans.

The analysis team weighed other landing criteria with specific Artemis III science objectives, including the goal to land close enough to a permanently shadowed region to allow crew to conduct a moonwalk, while limiting disturbance when landing. This will allow crew to collect samples and conduct scientific analysis in an uncompromised area, yielding important information about the depth, distribution, and composition of water ice that was confirmed at the Moon’s South Pole.

The team identified regions that can fulfill the moonwalk objective by ensuring proximity to permanently shadowed regions, and also factored in other lighting conditions. All 13 regions contain sites that provide continuous access to sunlight throughout a 6.5-day period – the planned duration of the Artemis III surface mission. Access to sunlight is critical for a long-term stay at the Moon because it provides a power source and minimizes temperature variations.

Several of the proposed sites within the regions are located among some of the oldest parts of the Moon, and together with the permanently shadowed regions, provide the opportunity to learn about the history of the Moon through previously unstudied lunar materials. 

NASA will select sites within regions for Artemis III after it identifies the mission’s target launch dates, which dictate transfer trajectories and surface environment conditions.

docs.title: Endurance-A Concept Azimuth Filter Path Coverage
docs.description: This layer represents the NAC coverage along the Endurance-A concept path that overlap and have a similar azimuth. When creating mosaics, lighting conditions should be similar for best results. Ideally difference in azimuth should not be more than a 20-degree difference. All 8,999 NACs have been filtered by azimuths of 165° ≤ to ≤ 185°. There are 1,282 fit the solar azimuth angle constrains resulting in 66.7% of the path covered with images within this filtering constraint.

docs.title: Endurance-A Concept Emission Filter Path Coverage
docs.description: This layer represents all overlapping NACs along the Endurance-A concept path in which the emission angles of the overlaps varied by over 2 degrees. It is recommended to have an emission angle difference of at least 2 degrees over overlapping images to create DEMs. Approximately 14.8% of the path is covered when considering emission angle variance.

docs.title: Endurance-A Concept NAC Crater Path Coverage
docs.description: This layer represents NAC coverage along the Endurance-A concept path that would be most suitable for crater detection. It is recommended to have a solar incidence angle between 50° and 75° for best crater detection results. Approximately 77.5% of the path is covered when considering incidence angle constraints.

docs.title: Endurance-A Concept NAC Cropped Footprint Path Coverage
docs.description: This layer represents the NAC coverage along the Endurance-A concept path that are within 0° < incidence < 90° and 0° ≤ emission ≤ 25°. A total of 8,999 NAC strips cover the traverse path. This layer has been cropped to fit a 2km distance around the path to ensure overlapping images are constrained to overlap on the path.

docs.title: Endurance-A Concept NAC Footprint Path Coverage
docs.description: This layer represents the NAC coverage along the Endurance-A concept path that are within 0° < incidence < 90° and 0° ≤ emission ≤ 25°. A total of 8,999 NAC strips cover the traverse path.

docs.title: Endurance-A Concept NAC Overlap Path Coverage
docs.description: This layer represents the NAC pair overlaps along the Endurance-A concept path. The path exhibits 32.65% NAC overlap coverage. Note that while the path looks entirely covered, the close-up on the right shows the path contains many gaps with no coverage.

docs.title: Endurance-A Concept NAC Rock Path Coverage
docs.description: This layer represents NAC coverage along the Endurance-A concept path that would be most suitable for rock detection. It is recommended to have a solar incidence angle between 65° and 85° for best rock detection results. Approximately 98.1% of the path is covered when considering incidence angle constraints.

docs.title: Endurance-A Concept NAC Unfiltered Path Coverage
docs.description: This layer represents the NAC coverage along the Endurance-A concept path that are within 0° < incidence < 90° and 0° ≤ emission ≤ 25°. A total of 8,999 NAC strips cover the traverse path. From these NAC strips we find all regions along the traverse with multiple strips that overlap. This results in 94.85% of the path has multiple image overlap.

docs.title: Endurance-A Concept Path, Version 1
docs.description: Endurance is a mission concept for a long-range rover (capable of traversing nearly 2,000 km) designed to explore and ultimately collect, cache, and return 12 samples from the South Pole-Aitken (SPA) basin on the farside of the Moon. SPA is the largest and oldest (undisputed) impact basin on the Moon, and holds critical answers to Solar System chronology and planetary evolution. For the science stations selected along the Southern traverse a traversable path between each of these sites was constructed. This path accounts for several conditions including: solar illumination (lighting), topography, slope, rocks, craters, and communication windows.

docs.title: Endurance-A Concept Path, Version 2
docs.description:
Endurance is a mission concept for a long-range rover (capable of traversing nearly 2,000 km) designed to explore and ultimately collect, cache, and return 12 samples from the South Pole-Aitken (SPA) basin on the farside of the Moon. SPA is the largest and oldest (undisputed) impact basin on the Moon, and holds critical answers to Solar System chronology and planetary evolution. For the science stations selected along the Southern traverse a traversable path between each of these sites was constructed. This path accounts for several conditions including: solar illumination (lighting), topography, slope, rocks, craters, and communication windows.

UPDATE: This path represents updates as of 04/11/2024. This path has been regenerated to include the science site of interest Site B. This path has also been regenerated using primarily the highest resolution LOLA DEMs (community standard reference) where available and LOLA+Kaguya DEM data elsewhere. DEM data used has been acquired from the PDS. Each DEM only exhibits coverage to certain extents. As such, the LOLA DEM resolution coverage for each extent is: 5m/px = 87.5S, 10m/px = 85S, 20m/px = 80S, 30m/px = 75S, and 60m/px = 60S. LOLA+ Kaguya had been used for portions of the path above 60S. This path has been color coded to visualize the portion of the path that has been generated using the different resolution DEMs. All DEMs were converted to slope maps and values > 15º were masked out as hazards; excluding these areas from path generation. This path also reflects a slight change of Site 007 location from it’s previous location to -88.695688,140.055726 since the previous location was on a pixel that exhibited > 15º slope according to the LOLA 5m/px DEM data.

docs.title: Endurance-A Concept Point Lighting Path Coverage
docs.description: This layer represents the percent lighting received along the Endurance-A concept path. Sun visibility has been computed every 10km along the path over the period of 28 days (09/01/2029 - 09/28/2029).

docs.title: Endurance-A Concept Science Stations, Version 1
docs.description: Endurance is a mission concept for a long-range rover (capable of traversing nearly 2,000 km) designed to explore and ultimately collect, cache, and return 12 samples from the South Pole-Aitken (SPA) basin on the farside of the Moon. SPA is the largest and oldest (undisputed) impact basin on the Moon, and holds critical answers to Solar System chronology and planetary evolution. Science station regions were determined by the science team setting about identifying specific candidate sample sites. These sites ranged from generalized regions (e.g., Site O: sample the ejecta of Lyman), to sites defined by single pixels of remote sensing data (e.g., Site C: sample the highest thorium anomaly outside of Abbe M crater; Site F: sample noritic material identified by M3). Details about these sites are displayed by clicking each science station on the map.

docs.description: This is a 50cm/px uncontrolled visible image mosaic generated using Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter Camera (LROC) Narrow Angle Camera (NAC) images from the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter mission. docs.title: Lunar Anthropogenic Impacts and Spacecraft Sites, S Pole
docs.description: This layer represents anthropogenic impacts and sSpacecraft sites associated with missions from all countries that have sent hardware to the lunar surface. This can help mission planning for their further landing sites to recognize areas of avoidance. Impactors represent the final disposition of the hardware on the surface and include missions intended as impacting missions, orbiters whose orbits decayed, failed landers, and jettisoned mission components. Note that particularly in the case of impactors, some missions where the impact sites location has a very high degree of uncertainty have been left out.  Others with significant but more moderate degrees of uncertainty are included and represented as circle. Data source: https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/planetary/lunar/lunar_artifact_impacts.html

docs.title: M3 Ice Exposures, South Polar
docs.description: This is a vector dataset depicting ice exposures for the south polar region of the Moon. Ice exposure detections are constrained by the Moon Mineralogy Mapper [M(3)], Lunar Orbiter Laser Altimeter (LOLA), Diviner Lunar Radiometer Experiment, and Lyman Alpha Mapping Project (LAMP) instruments. This data represents the distribution of water-ice-bearing pixels extending from approximately 75°S to 90°S. This data contains 1119 individual vector points, each associated with XY coordinates. Each vector point represents an M(3) pixel, ˜280m x 280m. The XY coordinates were plotted using ArcGIS and then reprojected to a south polar stereographic projection. This data was provided by: Shuai Li from the Department of Geology and Geophysics at the University of Hawaii.

docs.title: Permanently Shadowed Regions (PSRs), S Pole
docs.description: This data represents the XY coordinate location of Permanently Shadowed Regions (PSRs) as observed on the south pole. PSR observations range from ˜80°S to ˜90°S and are in a shapefile format. This dataset contains a total of 164 PSR observations, all > 10 km². A unique PSR ID is assigned to each PSR and are labeled accordingly; the first two characters represent the polar location (NP/SP), followed by the centroid latitude and then the centroid longitude. The values are separated by underscores and significant to, at most, 6 digits for latitude and 7 digits for longitude.

docs.title: Rock Fall Locations, South Pole
docs.description: This rockfall data represents the X, Y locations of rockfalls that have occurred at the south polar region of the Moon. The provided rockfall X, Y coordinates have been plotted, converted to shapefile format, and projected into a south polar stereographic projection. Rockfalls across the south polar lunar surface range in latitude from ˜85°S to ˜90°S exhibiting a relatively well-balanced distribution compared to the lunar near side, far side, and northern hemisphere regions. This data has been provided by and should be credited to Valentin Bickel et al. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-020-16653-3

docs.title: Unified Global Geologic Map of the Moon, Geologic Contacts
docs.description: Map description: This new work represents a seamless, globally consistent, 1:5,000,000-scale geologic map derived from the six digitally renovated geologic maps (see Source Online Linkage below). The goal of this project was to create a digital resource for science research and analysis, future geologic mapping efforts, be it local-, regional-, or global-scale products, and as a resource for the educators and the public interested in lunar geology. Here we present the completed mapping project as unit contacts, geologic unit polygons, linear features, and unit and feature nomenclature annotation. The product overlies shaded-relief products derived from SELENE Kaguya terrain camera stereo (equatorial, ˜60 m/pix) and LOLA altimetry (north and south polar, 100 m/pix). These data are not included with this download due to size considerations, but a readme in the Lunar_Raster folder provides the download links. This download page includes a PDF of the geologic map (right-side) with a brief Description of Map Units and Explanation of Map Symbols, as well as a JPG of the map for quick access viewing. This release is subject to update based on community feedback and peer-review. Version 2 updates: Two errors were addressed in this update: (1) Large area polygons were offset from their contacts, likely due to user error. Polygons were rebuilt to fix the issue and post processing (dissolving, reattributing, etc.) to rectify the aesthetic of the map. (2) Contacts were not visible but should have been due to incorrect labeling as DND (do not draw). Those that needed to be drawn have been reattributed as “certain” those that are not drawn are labeled as “internal”. Additionally, in version 1 of this data, crater polygons with similar attributes had been dissolved and lumped into contiguous units. This has been changed so that all craters are now discrete units. This adds ˜1000 units to the GeoUnits feature class and the related contacts are now visible and labeled as “certain”. Suggested citation: Fortezzo, C.M., Spudis, P. D. and Harrel, S. L. (2020). Release of the Digital Unified Global Geologic Map of the Moon At 1:5,000,000- Scale. Paper presented at the 51st Lunar and Planetary Science Conference, Lunar and Planetary Institute, Houston, TX. https://www.hou.usra.edu/meetings/lpsc2020/pdf/2760.pdf This map is for viewing purposes only. GIS files for this composite map can be found on the USGS Astropedia Lunar and Planetary Cartographic Catalog. Please note, this is not a USGS SIM. Map title: Unified Global Geologic Map of the Moon USGS Map Number: N/A Scale: 1:5M Authors: Fortezzo, C.M., Spudis, P. D. and Harrel, S. L. Publication date: 2020 Link to original map source: https://astrogeology.usgs.gov/search/map/Moon/Geology/Unified_Geologic_Map_of_the_Moon_GIS_v2
docs.instrument: Lunar Orbiter Laser Altimeter and Terrain Camera

docs.title: LRO NAC Orthoimage 0.66mpp, Endurance-A Concept Site Q
docs.description: This is an orthorectified LRO NAC image generated using AMES Stereo Pipeline and ISIS4. This data uses the NACs M110670656 and M110691019 as stereo image input. Output ortho image is sampled at 0.66mpp. Downloaded data is in a site centered orthographic projection. Data was created by: Heather Lethcoe at the Jet Propulsion Laboratory.

Hillshade was generated and color scheme has been applied using ArcGIS Pro. Downloaded data is in a site centered orthographic projection. Data was created by: Heather Lethcoe at the Jet Propulsion Laboratory.

docs.title: LRO NAC Crater Detections 0.83mpp, Endurance-A Concept Site Q
docs.description: This is an imagery mosaic of LRO NAC images that were used to generate crater detections for the Endurance-A Site Q region on the south pole of the moon. The crater detection tool takes a hybrid approach, which blends traditional computer vision techniques with deep learning. The input image is subsampled to various resolutions such that the base of the pyramid is the image at its highest resolution, and the apex of the pyramid is the image at its lowest resolution. The purpose for this structure is twofold; It allows for detection of craters at various sizes and it substantially decreases the processing time when searching for large craters. The output of tool includes a georeferenced image with craters labeled by bounding boxes.

docs.title: LRO LROC NAC Image Mosaic, S Pole
LRO LROC NAC Image Mosaic, S Pole, Avg Merge
LRO NAC Mosaic 1mpp, S Pole
docs.description:
This product is an uncontrolled mosaic of LROC NAC images of the South pole of the Moon, projected in Polar Stereographic with a scale of 1 m/px at the pole. The mosaic has a latitude range of 85.5 degrees to 90 degrees and is stored as 40 map tiles. The tiles are in latitudinal bands of 1 degrees, except for the polar tiles, which cover 1.5 degrees of latitude. There are four tiles in the first band (88.5 degrees to 90 degrees latitude), eight in the second (87.5 degrees to 88.5 degrees latitude), twelve in the third (86.5 degrees to 87.5 degrees latitude), and sixteen in the fourth (85.5 degrees to 86.5 degrees latitude). Due to the tilt of the Moon's spin axis (1.54 degrees), some regions near the poles are in permanent shadow while other nearby regions remain illuminated for the majority of the year. This subtle tilt causes lighting changes from lunation to lunation. The poles are most illuminated at their respective summer solstice. Thus images for this NAC south pole mosaic were acquired during the southern solstice (2010-07-23 through 2010-12-11), and layered in order of the greatest incidence angle and sub-solar latitude closest to the pole. All NAC images were map projected onto the LOLA polar DEM, sampled at 100 m/px, using the LOLA crossover-corrected ephemeris. All tiles use the same polar stereographic projection so they can be combined into a seamless mosaic without reprojection. The images were not registered to one another. The combined mosaic of these tiles has been manually tiepointed to the current basemap layer LRO LROC WAC Image Mosaic, S Pole.
When citing this product, use the following reference: Wagner, R. V., Speyerer, E. J., Robinson, M. S., & LROC Team. (2015). New Mosaicked Data Products from the LROC Team. In Lunar and Planetary Science Conference (Vol. 46, abstract #1473). https://www.hou.usra.edu/meetings/lpsc2015/pdf/1473.pdf

docs.title: LRO LOLA Color DEM Error 5 mpp, Site06: Nobile Rim 1, S Pole
docs.description: This is a colorized high-resolution Digital Elevation Model (DEM) of the high-priority lunar south pole landing site Nobile Rim 1 (Site 06). This DEM was generated using exclusively laser altimetry data acquired by LRO-LOLA and through an iterative co-adjustment of the LOLA tracks in a self-consistent fashion. This reduced the orbital errors by over a factor of 10 such that the new track geolocation uncertainty is ˜10 - 20 cm horizontally and ˜2 - 4 cm vertically. This new 5m/px DEM is substantially more realistic than previous ones with fewer artifacts due to orbital errors and fewer spurious noise points. While the fraction of interpolated 5m pixels in these polar LDEMs is necessarily large (˜90&percnt) due to LOLA's cross-track and inter-spot spacing, these LDEMs have the advantage of having accurate geodetic control and of being unaffected by shadows, and, thus, will be useful constraints on higher-resolution topographic models derived from imagery. The elevation values are in meters and are relative to a radius of 1737400m. Please site the following when using this data: Barker, M.K., et al. (2020), Improved LOLA Elevation Maps for South Pole Landing Sites: Error Estimates and Their Impact on Illumination Conditions, Planetary & Space Science, in press, doi:10.1016/j.pss.2020.105119.

docs.title: LRO LOLA Color DEM Error 5 mpp, Site20: Leibnitz Beta Plateau, S Pole
docs.description: This data represents the colorized total Z uncertainty in meters (formally, the RMS error) for the high-resolution Digital Elevation Model (DEM) of the high-priority lunar south pole landing site Leibnitz beta plateau (Site 20). The total Z uncertainty has been derived by a method to estimate surface height uncertainty in the new LDEMs that accounts for the reduced orbital errors and interpolation errors. This method circumvents the infeasible computation of the full error-covariance matrix of the LDEM. Instead, we use the fractal nature of lunar topography to build a more computationally manageable statistical ensemble of clones with similar error properties as the data. Interpolation error depends primarily on gap size, or areal density of the LOLA points, with a secondary dependence on terrain slope that becomes more important over highly sloped terrain. Hence, the interpolation error will be larger at greater distances from the pole for the same pixel scale, because of the lower point density and poorer effective resolution. Please site the following when using this data: Barker, M.K., et al. (2020), Improved LOLA Elevation Maps for South Pole Landing Sites: Error Estimates and Their Impact on Illumination Conditions, Planetary & Space Science, in press, doi:10.1016/j.pss.2020.105119.

docs.title: LRO LOLA Color Slope < 10 deg, S Pole, 87.5 deg
docs.description: This is a colorized slope map that was generated from the version 4 of the LRO LOLA DEM, S Pole, 87.5 deg. The DEM is a shape map (radius) of the Moon at a resolution 5 m/px, based on altimetry data acquired through September 2011 by the LOLA instrument. The ground tracks were interpolated using the Generic Mapping Tools programs “surface” and “grdblend”. The DEM was scaled from a 16-bit signed integer to a 32-bit floating point. Slope was generated from this DEM to create this slope product sampled at 5 m/px. Slope values greater than 10 deg were excluded from this data for visualization and analysis purposes. Slope values are in degrees and referred to a radius of 1737400m. The legend conveys the mapping colors to slope values (degrees).

docs.title: LRO LOLA Color Slope Error 5 mpp, Site20: Leibnitz Beta Plateau, S Pole
docs.description: This data represents the colorized slope uncertainty in degrees (formally, the RMS error) for the high-resolution slope map of the high-priority lunar south pole landing site Leibnitz beta plateau (Site 20). The total Z uncertainty has been derived by a method to estimate surface height uncertainty in the new LDEMs that accounts for the reduced orbital errors and interpolation errors. This method circumvents the infeasible computation of the full error-covariance matrix of the LDEM. Instead, we use the fractal nature of lunar topography to build a more computationally manageable statistical ensemble of clones with similar error properties as the data. Interpolation error depends primarily on gap size, or areal density of the LOLA points, with a secondary dependence on terrain slope that becomes more important over highly sloped terrain. Hence, the interpolation error will be larger at greater distances from the pole for the same pixel scale, because of the lower point density and poorer effective resolution. Please site the following when using this data: Barker, M.K., et al. (2020), Improved LOLA Elevation Maps for South Pole Landing Sites: Error Estimates and Their Impact on Illumination Conditions, Planetary & Space Science, in press, doi:10.1016/j.pss.2020.105119.

docs.title: LRO LOLA DEM Error 5 mpp, Site20: Leibnitz Beta Plateau, S Pole
docs.description: This data represents the total Z uncertainty in meters (formally, the RMS error) for the high-resolution Digital Elevation Model (DEM) of the high-priority lunar south pole landing site Leibnitz beta plateau (Site 20). The total Z uncertainty has been derived by a method to estimate surface height uncertainty in the new LDEMs that accounts for the reduced orbital errors and interpolation errors. This method circumvents the infeasible computation of the full error-covariance matrix of the LDEM. Instead, we use the fractal nature of lunar topography to build a more computationally manageable statistical ensemble of clones with similar error properties as the data. Interpolation error depends primarily on gap size, or areal density of the LOLA points, with a secondary dependence on terrain slope that becomes more important over highly sloped terrain. Hence, the interpolation error will be larger at greater distances from the pole for the same pixel scale, because of the lower point density and poorer effective resolution. Please site the following when using this data: Barker, M.K., et al. (2020), Improved LOLA Elevation Maps for South Pole Landing Sites: Error Estimates and Their Impact on Illumination Conditions, Planetary & Space Science, in press, doi:10.1016/j.pss.2020.105119.

This DEM was generated using exclusively laser altimetry data acquired by LRO-LOLA and through an iterative co-adjustment of the LOLA tracks in a self-consistent fashion. This reduced the orbital errors by over a factor of 10 such that the new track geolocation uncertainty is ˜10 - 20 cm horizontally and ˜2 - 4 cm vertically. This new 5m/px DEM is substantially more realistic than previous ones with fewer artifacts due to orbital errors and fewer spurious noise points. While the fraction of interpolated 5m pixels in these polar LDEMs is necessarily large (˜90%) due to LOLA's cross-track and inter-spot spacing, these LDEMs have the advantage of having accurate geodetic control and of being unaffected by shadows, and, thus, will be useful constraints on higher-resolution topographic models derived from imagery. Slope values are in degrees and are relative to a radius of 1737400m. The legend conveys the mapping color to slope values (degrees). Please cite the following reference when using this data: Barker, M.K., et al. (2020), Improved LOLA Elevation Maps for South Pole Landing Sites: Error Estimates and Their Impact on Illumination Conditions, Planetary & Space Science, in press, doi:10.1016/j.pss.2020.105119.

docs.title: LRO LOLA Slope Error 5 mpp, Site20: Leibnitz Beta Plateau, S Pole
docs.description: This data represents the slope uncertainty in degrees (formally, the RMS error) for the high-resolution slope map of the high-priority lunar south pole landing site Leibnitz beta plateau (Site 20). The total Z uncertainty has been derived by a method to estimate surface height uncertainty in the new LDEMs that accounts for the reduced orbital errors and interpolation errors. This method circumvents the infeasible computation of the full error-covariance matrix of the LDEM. Instead, we use the fractal nature of lunar topography to build a more computationally manageable statistical ensemble of clones with similar error properties as the data. Interpolation error depends primarily on gap size, or areal density of the LOLA points, with a secondary dependence on terrain slope that becomes more important over highly sloped terrain. Hence, the interpolation error will be larger at greater distances from the pole for the same pixel scale, because of the lower point density and poorer effective resolution. Please site the following when using this data: Barker, M.K., et al. (2020), Improved LOLA Elevation Maps for South Pole Landing Sites: Error Estimates and Their Impact on Illumination Conditions, Planetary & Space Science, in press, doi:10.1016/j.pss.2020.105119.

docs.title: LRO LOLA Slope, S Pole, 87.5 deg
docs.description: This is a slope map that was generated from the version 4 of the LRO LOLA DEM, S Pole, 87.5 deg. The DEM is a shape map (radius) of the Moon at a resolution 5 m/px, based on altimetry data acquired through September 2011 by the LOLA instrument. The ground tracks were interpolated using the Generic Mapping Tools programs “surface” and “grdblend”. The DEM was scaled from a 16-bit signed integer to a 32-bit floating point. Slope was generated from this DEM to create this slope product sampled at 5 m/px. Slope values are in degrees and referred to a radius of 1737400m. The legend conveys the mapping colors to slope values (degrees).

docs.title: LRO Narrow Angle Camera, DEM Schrodinger Vent
docs.description: This is a 5m/px digita elevation model (DEM) generated using Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter Camera (LROC) Narrow Angle Camera (NAC) stereo images and Lunar Orbiter Laser Alimeter(LOLA) shot points from the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LRO) mission. Each NAC stereopair was processed to create a multiple DEMs,each DEM was aligned tointersecting LOLA shot points, and merged into a sigle DEM using AIMES Stereo Pipeline.

docs.title: CE-2 CCD Ortho Mosaic, S Pole
docs.description:
China's Chang'e 2 robotic probe was launched from Xichang Satellite Launch Center on 1 October 2010 aboard a Long March 3C rocket. It conducted studies of the Moon’s surface from lunar orbit between October 6 2010 and June 8 2011, prior to continuing its mission at the Earth-Sun L2 Lagrangian point and the asteroid Toutatis. From its working orbit with an altitude of 100 km above the lunar surface, Chang'e 2 was able to produce a global map of the Moon with 7-meter resolution, the highest-resolution map of the entire Moon to have been yet produced. It is this 7-meter data that was used to produce this layer in Moon Trek. Chang'e 2 also worked from an elliptical orbit with a perilune of 15 km and an apolune of apolune, allowing selected areas to be imaged at resolutions as high as 1.3 meters, enabling higher-resolution mapping of areas targeted for future landings.

Chang'e 2’s CCD camera employs a two-line push-broom sensor. The two CCD lines are positioned on separate focal planes, enabling the gathering of forward- and backward-looking imagery along the line of flight. This allows for the simultaneous production of stereo pairs. Both lines consist of 6144 10.1 µm pixels. Because the forward-looking line is closer to the center of the focal plane, it offers better resolution with a viewing angle of 8°, while the rear-looking line has a viewing angle of 17.2°.

On April 4, 2018, the CE-2 Global Digital Orthophoto Model (DOM) dataset with 7m resolution was released by Ground Research and Application System of China Lunar Exploration Program. The dataset is produced using images acquired by CCD stereo cameras onboard CE-2 spacecraft at 100 km orbit, which is divided into 844 map subdivisions. 

Individual map subdivision tiles were mosaicked together and clipped at the south polar region from 90S to 60S. This data has been projected to a stereographic polar projection. This data is an 8-bit unsigned integer with values ranging from 1 to 255 and a no data value of 0.

docs.title: LROC NAC Uncontrolled Mosaic of Schrodinger Crater, 10m/px
docs.description: This is a 10m/px uncontrolled visible image mosaic generated using Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter Camera (LROC) Narrow Angle Camera (NAC) images from the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter mission. Each NAC image was registered horizontally to the LRO's Lunar Orbiter Laser Altimeter (LOLA) global DEM, and then mosaicked together and color balanced.

docs.title: LRO Mini-RF CPR 15mpp, Malapert
docs.description:
This is a Mini-RF Circularly Polarized Ratio (CPR) dataset with the 49 degrees equivalent incidence angle trend removed. Data units are in Decibels (db) where bright pixels (greater than 0 db) represent relatively high backscatter and dark pixels (less than 0 db) represent low backscatter.

Mini-RF is a Synthetic Aperture Radar designed in a hybrid dual-polarimetric architecture, transmitting a circularly polarized signal to the lunar surface and receives the horizontal and vertical linear polarizations. The received radar signal from Mini-RF is represented using the four Stokes parameters, which can be combined to derive metrics for lunar surface properties. The monostatic Mini-RF data in the PDS was processed onto a spherical Moon, and the applied Vexcel SAR processor resulted in offsets to the correct selenolocation (see Harris et al., this meeting). As a result, until now, local incidence angles were not known for the monostatic data. We have corrected the position of level-1 monostatic S-band data & re-orthorectified it on to a SLDEM/LOLA shape model. The local incidence angle of each pixel can then be determined. The observed trend in CPR for the monostatic data agrees reasonably well with expectations from Hagfors modeling, at least for i˜35° and ˜70°, with a dielectric permittivity of ˜4.3. Removal of this CPR trend emphasizes deviations from typical scattering properties. Data Credit: https://www.hou.usra.edu/meetings/lpsc2023/pdf/1564.pdf

docs.title: LRO NAC PSR Mosaic 20mpp, S Pole
docs.description: This is an uncontrolled mosaic generated from images taken by the Narrow Angle Camera (NAC) onboard the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LRO) for the South Pole region of the Moon. The NAC mosaics have been trimmed to the Permanently Shadowed Region (PSR) shapefile, providing visible NAC image coverage of the PSRs only. Acquisition of NAC PSR observations were optimized over several campaigns to maximize signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), resulting in a comprehensive dataset that is systematically reviewed and analyzed. Observations are acquired at a variety of pixel scales (2 to 20 m/px). The final PSR mosaics are assembled from re-sampled images to 20 m/px, and ordering of images is based on image quality and areal coverage of individual PSRs. A total of 550 NAC images were used to create a South Pole PSR mosaic at 20 m/px, 90° to 80° latitude, and -180° to 180° longitude. This mosaic has been merged with the existing LROC NAC South Pole RDR product to replace over-saturated illuminated polar areas.

docs.title: Chandrayaan-1 Mini-SAR CPR S Pole
docs.description: This is the Mini-SAR CPR dataset. Mini-SAR combines synthetic aperture radar (SAR) at two wavelengths (S and X band) and two resolutions (150 m and 30 m) with interferometric and communications. Previous radar observations (Earth-based, and one bistatic data set from Clementine) of the permanently shadowed regions of the lunar poles seem to indicate areas of high circular polarization ratio (CPR) consistent with volume scattering from volatile deposits (e.g. water ice) buried at shallow (0.1-1 m) depth. Between mid-February and mid-April, 2009, Mini-SAR mapped more than 95% of the areas polewards of 80° latitude at a resolution of 150 meters. The north polar region displays backscatter properties typical for the Moon, with circular polarization ratio (CPR) values in the range of 0.1-0.3, increasing to over 1.0 for young primary impact craters. These higher CPR values likely reflect surface roughness associated with these fresh features. In contrast, some craters in this region show elevated CPR in their interiors, but not exterior to their rims. Almost all of these features are in permanent sun shadow and correlate with proposed locations of polar ice modeled on the basis of Lunar Prospector neutron data. These relations are consistent with deposits of water ice in these craters. The CPR is derived from the Stokes parameters. This map is not ortho-rectified.

docs.title: LRO WAC Mosaic, S Pole v2
LRO WAC Percentage-Based Illumination 100mpp, S Pole
docs.description: The Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter Camera (LROC) provides multi-temporal images of the polar regions, with repeat imaging with the Wide-Angle Camera approximately every 2 hours with a ground sampling distance of 100 meters enabling production of an illumination map from 88 to 90 degrees south. WAC images (n=3807) acquired over one lunar year from 15 February 2010 to 5 February 2011 form the basis of the map. Temporal gaps were filled with 229 observations acquired with virtually identical lighting at other times during the mission. Each image was first map-projected at 100 meters/pixel in polar stereographic projection onto a 30 m LOLA DEM (Smith et al., 2010) using an improved WAC distortion model (Speyerer et al., 2016) and improved spacecraft ephemeris (Mazarico et al., 2011). Binary images indicating the illumination state of each image were created by applying a series of spatial filters and a conservative global threshold. Then the illumination map was derived by taking the number of times a mapped pixel was illuminated over the number of instances the mapped pixel was imaged. This map may contain some biases due to non-uniform timing between observations (Example- WAC images were not acquired on orbits when Mini-RF acquired polar observations). To limit this non-linear effect, an additional time-weighted illumination map is provided that linearly interpolated missed observations (see WAC_POLE_ILL_TWI_NORTH and WAC_POLE_ILL_TWI_SOUTH). For more information on the derivation of these products and for a map of image counts per pixel, see Speyerer and Robinson (2013). Due to a small amount of image noise and scattered light, some regions that are permanently shadowed from direct solar illumination have percentage values that are close to, but not equal to zero. These artifacts in the middle of permanently shadowed regions should be ignored when analyzing the extent. When citing this product, use the following reference: Speyerer, E. J., & Robinson, M. S. (2013). Persistently illuminated regions at the lunar poles: Ideal sites for future exploration. Icarus, 222(1), 122-136. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.icarus.2012.10.010

docs.title: LRO WAC Time-Weighted Illumination 100mpp, S Pole
docs.description: The Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter Camera (LROC) provides multi-temporal images of the polar regions, with repeat imaging with the Wide-Angle Camera approximately every 2 hours with a ground sampling distance of 100 meters enabling production of an illumination map from 88 to 90 degrees south. To create the polar illumination map, WAC images acquired over one lunar year from 15 February 2010 to 5 February 2011 were used, resulting in 3807 observations. Temporal gaps were filled with 229 observations acquired with virtually identical lighting at other times during the mission. Each image was first map-projected at 100 meters/pixel in polar stereographic projection onto a 30 m DEM provided by the LOLA team (Smith et al., 2010) using an improved WAC distortion model (Speyerer et al., 2016) and improved spacecraft ephemeris (Mazarico et al., 2011). Binary images indicating the illumination state of each image were created by applying a series of spatial filters and a conservative global threshold. Like the percentage-based illumination maps, this illumination map was derived by taking the number of times a mapped pixel was illuminated over the number of instances the mapped pixel was imaged. However, in order to minimize biases introduced by non-equally spaced observations, images taken during periods of infrequent WAC observations are weighted twice as much as those taken during nominal operations and areas not within the field of view were linearly interpolated based on preceding and subsequent observations where image data was available for a specific mapped pixel. A version of the illumination map without interpolation is archived under WAC_POLE_ILL_PCT_NORTH and WAC_POLE_ILL_PCT_SOUTH. For more information on the derivation of these products and for a map of image counts per pixel, see Speyerer and Robinson (2013). Due to a small amount of image noise and scattered light, some regions that are permanently shadowed from direct solar illumination have percentage values that are close to, but not equal to zero. These artifacts in the middle of permanently shadowed regions should be ignored when analyzing the extent. When citing this product, use the following reference: Speyerer, E. J., & Robinson, M. S. (2013). Persistently illuminated regions at the lunar poles: Ideal sites for future exploration. Icarus, 222(1), 122-136. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.icarus.2012.10.010

docs.description: This is a colorized global rock abundance map of the south pole region of the lunar surface at 128 pixels per degree. This data is a Level 3 derived Gridded Data Record (GDR) and only contains data collected from October 3, 2009 through October 7, 2011, which corresponds to the mapping orbit phase of the LRO mission.  These data were acquired during near-circular orbits at ˜50 km altitude, which are generally lower altitudes than (typical) elliptical orbits. All GDRs: Each sample represents the areal fraction of the surface covered by rock fragments as estimated using the original algorithm described in Bandfield et al. (2011) with improvements to the algorith accounting for local slopes described in Bandfield et al. (2016). Values are scaled by the value of SCALING_FACTOR. Conversion from Digital Number (DN) to average is given by the equation: RA = (DN * SCALING_FACTOR) + OFFSET Data were restricted to local times or 1930 to 0530 with the solar incidence angles greater than 90 degrees, latitudes between 80N and 80S, emission angles less than 15 degrees, brightness temperatures less than 200K. Local slopes are taken into account using the LROC 128ppd DEM to adjust nighttime rock temperatures used in the model. Several data quality constraints were used as well (quality flag for calibration, 0; quality flag for miscellaneous, 0; noise quality flag, 0 to 1). Gridded level 2 data from diviner spectral channels 6, 7, and 8 binned at 128 pixels per degree. Because of the groundtrack walk and local time drift of Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter observations, most surfaces are covered by only a single observation.  In some cases, surfaces are covered by multiple observations acquired ˜6 or 12 months apart.

The DEM is a shape map (radius) of the Moon at a resolution of 128 pixels per degree, based on altimetry data acquired through September 2011 by the LOLA instrument. The ground tracks were interpolated using the Generic Mapping Tools programs surface and grdblend. The map is in the form of a binary table with one row for each 0.007813 degree of latitude, pixel registered. Map values are referred to a radius of 1737400 m.

docs.title: LRO Mini-RF CPR, S Pole v2
docs.description: This dataset is the Mini-RF Circular Polarization Ratio (CPR) data product. CPR is defined as the ratio of the same sense circular polarization to the opposite sense circular polarization (CPR = SC / OS). The Level 3 products are Derived Data Records (DDRs) generated from multiple Level 2 CDRs.  They are mosaics that are produced by ingesting the Level 2 Stokes 1 parameter and circular polarization files into the ISIS software.  The mosaics are produced for entire lunar globe (i.e., regions between -180 and 180 longitude and -90 to 90 latitude). Unlike the lower-level products, these are composed of data sets collected during multiple acquisitions and are produced manually using the ISIS software provided by the Astrogeology branch of the USGS. The original global dataset was obtained from the Planetary Data System (PDS) at a resolution of 128ppd. The global mosaic was clipped to an extent of -180 to 180 and -60 to -90 and then a south polar stereographic projection was applied. This data has a value range from 0 to 1.

docs.title: Ice Stability at Depth Paleo SP
docs.description: The Diviner imaging radiometer experiment aboard the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter has revealed that surface temperatures in parts of the lunar polar regions are among the lowest in the solar system. Moreover, modeling of these Diviner data using realistic thermal conductivity profiles for lunar regolith and topography-based illumination reveals that large expanses of circumpolar terrain could have near-subsurface temperatures well below 110K, despite receiving episodic low-angle solar illumination. These subsurface cold traps could provide areally extensive reservoirs of volatiles. Thermal model results can be used to estimate the stability of water ice deposits to loss by sublimation and diffusive migration through the lunar regolith and map of the depths at which water ice would be lost at a rate of less than 1 kg m-2 per billion years, which corresponds to a loss rate of 1 mm per billion years for a pure ice deposit. The results show that surface cold traps for water ice are surrounded by much more extensive “lunar permafrost” regions where water ice is stable in close proximity to the surface. However, the polar hydrogen deposits mapped by orbiting neutron spectrometers and their observed spatial distribution does not match the expected distribution of water ice inferred from present-day lunar temperatures. This distribution of polar hydrogen preserves evidence that the spin axis of the Moon has shifted, in what is termed true polar wander. This map shows Matt Siegler's calculation of the ice stability depth when the ancient pole was offset toward Cabeus, before true polar wander took place. [Paige, D. A., et al. (2010), Diviner observations of cold traps in the lunar south polar region: Spatial distribution and temperature, Science,330,479–482; Elphic, R, et al. (2011). Limits on the Abundance and Burial Depth of Lunar Polar Ice. AGU Fall Meeting Abstracts; Siegler, M.A, et al. (2016), Lunar true polar wander inferred from polar hydrogen, Nature 531, 480–484]

docs.title: LRO DLRE Seasonal Difference Max Temp, S Pole
docs.description:
This is the seasonal difference in maximum temperature on the south pole of the Moon. This data was created by subtracting the maximum winter temperature data from the maximum summer temperature data. This data has been obtained from the Diviner instrument onboard the Lunar Reconnaissance Obiter (LRO) and is sampled at 240 m/px. The Diviner Lunar Radiometer Experiment is a nine-channel infrared radiometer employing filter radiometry. These channels are distributed between two identical, boresighted telescopes, and an articulated elevation/azimuth mount allows the telescopes to view the lunar surface, space, and calibration targets. The instantaneous field-of-view (FOV) response of each channel is defined by a linear, 21-element, thermopile detector array at the telescope focal plane, and its spectral response is defined by a focal plane bandpass filter. Diviner nadir-pointing RDR data from July, 5, 2009 to Feb 17, 2019 has been compiled into polar stereographic maps of temperatures poleward of 80 degrees latitude at fixed local times and fixed subsolar longitudes to provide an overview of diurnal temperatures of the polar regions. The data has been divided into winter and summer seasons, defined by the times of year when the subsolar latitude is above or below the equator, to characterize the variations in seasonal temperatures that result from the 1.54 degree angle between the Moon's spin pole and the ecliptic plane.

Reference:  Williams, J.-P., B. T. Greenhagen, D. A. Paige, N. Schorghofer, E. Sefton-Nash, P. O. Hayne, P. G. Lucey, M. A. Siegler, and K.-Michael Aye (2019) Seasonal polar temperatures on the Moon, Journal of Geophysical Research, 124, 2505-2521, https://doi.org/10.1029/2019JE006028.

docs.title: LRO LAMP Albedo S Pole, Color
LRO LOLA Average Earth Visibility, 240 mpp, S Pole
docs.description: This data represents the Earth visibility, averaged over hourly timesteps spanning 18.6 years, for the South Polar region of the Moon. Since our light source is not a point but rather a finite disc, its position and size can be changed to study the visibility of the Earth from the lunar poles rather than the solar input. The extent of this data has been clipped to 60S-90S and has a resolution of 240 m/px. Pixel values represent the percentage of Earth visibility and the legend coveys the mapping colors to values. When using this data please cite: Mazarico, E., et al. (2011), Illumination conditions of the lunar polar regions using LOLA topography, Icarus, Vol. 211, pp. 1066-1081, doi:10.1016/j.icarus.2010.10.030.

docs.title: Kaguya SP Clinopyroxene Abundance SP
docs.description:
This is a map of polar Clinopyroxene abundance. Quantitative lunar polar mineral abundance maps were derived by comparing continuum-removed Kaguya Spectral Profiler (SP) reflectance spectra between 742.8 and 1555.5 nm, to continuum-removed spectra modeled using radiative transfer equations (which describe the scattering of light interacting with intimately mixed particles larger than the wavelength). A composition was then assigned to each SP point by searching for the best spectral match, ensuring that the best spectral fit contains within +/-5 wt.% FeO of the given SP point. FeO abundances were determined using SP and LOLA data as described for the Polar FeO Abundance Maps by Lemelin, et al. (MINERALOGY AND IRON CONTENT OF THE LUNAR POLAR REGIONS USING THE KAGUYA SPECTRAL PROFILER AND THE LUNAR ORBITER LASER ALTIMETER. M. Lemelin, P. G. Lucey, K. Jha, and D. Trang, Lunar and Planetary Science XLVIII, 2017)

The Kaguya Spectral Profiler was a nadir looking visible - near infrared spectrometer onboard the Japanese SELENE (Kaguya) lunar explorer launched in September 2007. SP consisted of one reflective telescope, two plane gratings, three linear detectors, one three-stage peltier cooler, and two halogen lamps with a filter for radiometric and spectral calibration. Its spectral coverage and sampling interval, 0.5 - 2.6 !m and 6 - 8 nm, were optimized for the detection of spectral absorption features of lunar surface minerals. The along-track sampling interval was 500 m. The total number of SP's spectral channels was 296 including several overlapping channels around 1 micrometer.

docs.title: LRO LOLA and Kaguya SP FeO Abundance SP
docs.description:
This is a map of polar iron oxide (FeO) abundance. FeO maps of the polar regions (50-90 degree in latitude) at 1 km per pixel were derived by taking advantage of calibrated reflectance data at 1064 nm from the Lunar Orbiter Laser Altimeter (LOLA) and using it along with the 955.5/752.8 nm reflectance ratio from the Kaguya Spectral Profiler (SP). (MINERALOGY AND IRON CONTENT OF THE LUNAR POLAR REGIONS USING THE KAGUYA SPECTRAL PROFILER AND THE LUNAR ORBITER LASER ALTIMETER. M. Lemelin, P. G. Lucey, K. Jha3, and D. Trang, Lunar and Planetary Science XLVIII, 2017)

The Kaguya Spectral Profiler was a nadir looking visible - near infrared spectrometer onboard the Japanese SELENE (Kaguya) lunar explorer launched in September 2007. SP consisted of one reflective telescope, two plane gratings, three linear detectors, one three-stage peltier cooler, and two halogen lamps with a filter for radiometric and spectral calibration. The Lunar Orbiter Laser Altimeter (LOLA) aboart the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter has been actively acquiring reflectance data of the Moon since 2009; it sends a laser pulse towards the Moon at 1064 nm and measures the energy returned from the surface at 0 degree phase angle, regardless of the Sun’s illumination conditions. It provides high signal to noise ratio for the entire lunar surface, regardless of topography, and has been thoroughly calibrated and gridded into polar maps of 1 km per pixel.

docs.title: GRAIL LGRS, Bouguer Disturbances L1200
docs.description: This data product is a map of the   Bouguer disturbances (in mGal) of the lunar gravity field at a resolution  of 16 pix/deg by 16 pix/deg. It is based on a GRAIL gravity field of the Moon  produced by NASA GSFC called GRGM1200A. GRGM1200A is a degree and order 1200  spherical harmonic model, which includes the entire mission of GRAIL tracking  data. The LOLA topography, expressed in the Principal Axes frame, was used to  remove the contribution of the lunar relief (assuming a constant density of  2500 kg/m3). The Bouguer disturbances are expanded in the spatial domain up   to degree and order 1200.   Some details describing this model are:    The spherical harmonic coefficients are fully normalized (geodesy 4pi    normalized).    The uncertainties are calibrated (the formal uncertainties multiplied by    a factor of 1.635).    The reference radius = 1738.0 km    The gravitational parameter is GM = 4902.80011526323 km**3/s**2    The planetary ephemeris used is de430 and defines the lunar body-fixed        coordinate system.    A Kaula type power law constraint is applied to the spherical harmonics        coefficients for degrees >600 (3.6e-4/n^2).    The weighting of the KBRR data is:        0.03 microns/sec in the primary mission        0.05 microns/sec in the extended mission    The weighting of the DSN data is:        0.12mm/s in both the primary and extended mission   The nominal tidal Love number is k2 = 0.024133 +/- 0.000016   The current best reference for the GRGM1200A gravity field is  LEMOINEETAL2014, published in the Geophysical Research Letters with the  DOI number 10.1002/2014GL060027 . For additional details on the GRAIL  mission, data and methods, see LEMOINEETAL2013.     Each point gives the Lunar Bouguer gravity disturbance in milligals,    on a reference sphere with semi-major-axis = 1738.0 km,    GM = 4902.80011526323 km**3/s**2, and zero rotation rate.   As with other lunar gravity fields, the map is expressed in the Moon  Principal Axes frame, which slightly differs from the Moon Mean Earth frame.  For comparison with lunar topography, users are advised to make use of   the LOLA PDS products also archived in the Moon Principal Axes frame, such  as the LDEM_64_PA product in the LRO-L-LOLA-4-GDR-V1.0 dataset, which   can be accessed at the PDS Geosciences Node or at the LOLA PDS Data node.  Note also that the reference radius for gravity (1738 km) and topography  (1737.4 km) are different."

docs.description: This data product is a map of the   gravity anomalies (in mGal) of the lunar gravity field at a resolution     of 16 pix/deg by 16 pix/deg. It is based on a GRAIL gravity field of the Moon  produced by NASA GSFC called GRGM1200A. GRGM1200A is a degree and order 1200  spherical harmonic model, which includes the entire mission of GRAIL tracking  data. The anomalies are expanded in the spatial domain up to degree and order  180.   Some details describing this model are:    The spherical harmonic coefficients are fully normalized (geodesy 4pi    normalized).    The uncertainties are calibrated (the formal uncertainties multiplied by    a factor of 1.635).    The reference radius = 1738.0 km    The gravitational parameter is GM = 4902.80011526323 km**3/s**2    The planetary ephemeris used is de430 and defines the lunar body-fixed        coordinate system.    A Kaula type power law constraint is applied to the spherical harmonics        coefficients for degrees >600 (3.6e-4/n^2).    The weighting of the KBRR data is:        0.03 microns/sec in the primary mission        0.05 microns/sec in the extended mission    The weighting of the DSN data is:        0.12mm/s in both the primary and extended mission   The nominal tidal Love number is k2 = 0.024133 +/- 0.000016   The current best reference for the GRGM1200A gravity field is  LEMOINEETAL2014, published in the Geophysical Research Letters with the  DOI number 10.1002/2014GL060027 . For additional details on the GRAIL  mission, data and methods, see LEMOINEETAL2013.     Each point gives the Lunar gravity anomaly in milligals,    on a reference sphere with semi-major-axis = 1738.0 km,    GM = 4902.80011526323 km**3/s**2, and zero rotation rate.   As other lunar gravity fields, the map is expressed in the Moon Principal  Axes frame, which slightly differs from the Moon Mean Earth frame.  For comparison with lunar topography, users are advised to make use of   the LOLA PDS products also archived in the Moon Principal Axes frame, such  as the LDEM_64_PA product in the LRO-L-LOLA-4-GDR-V1.0 dataset, which   can be accessed at the PDS Geosciences Node or at the LOLA PDS Data node.  Note also that the reference radius for gravity (1738 km) and topography  (1737.4 km) are different.

GRGM1200A is a degree and order 1200  spherical harmonic model, which includes the entire mission of GRAIL tracking  data. The disturbances are expanded in the spatial domain up to degree and  order 180.   Some details describing this model are:    The spherical harmonic coefficients are fully normalized (geodesy 4pi    normalized).    The uncertainties are calibrated (the formal uncertainties multiplied by    a factor of 1.635).    The reference radius = 1738.0 km    The gravitational parameter is GM = 4902.80011526323 km**3/s**2    The planetary ephemeris used is de430 and defines the lunar body-fixed        coordinate system.    A Kaula type power law constraint is applied to the spherical harmonics        coefficients for degrees >600 (3.6e-4/n^2).    The weighting of the KBRR data is:        0.03 microns/sec in the primary mission        0.05 microns/sec in the extended mission    The weighting of the DSN data is:        0.12mm/s in both the primary and extended mission   The nominal tidal Love number is k2 = 0.024133 +/- 0.000016   The current best reference for the GRGM1200A gravity field is  LEMOINEETAL2014, published in the Geophysical Research Letters with the  DOI number 10.1002/2014GL060027 . For additional details on the GRAIL  mission, data and methods, see LEMOINEETAL2013.     Each point gives the Lunar gravity disturbance in milligals,    on a reference sphere with semi-major-axis = 1738.0 km,    GM = 4902.80011526323 km**3/s**2, and zero rotation rate.   As other lunar gravity fields, the map is expressed in the Moon Principal  Axes frame, which slightly differs from the Moon Mean Earth frame.  For comparison with lunar topography, users are advised to make use of   the LOLA PDS products also archived in the Moon Principal Axes frame, such  as the LDEM_64_PA product in the LRO-L-LOLA-4-GDR-V1.0 dataset, which   can be accessed at the PDS Geosciences Node or at the LOLA PDS Data node.  Note also that the reference radius for gravity (1738 km) and topography  (1737.4 km) are different.

docs.title: LRO DLRE Bolometric Brightness Max Temperature Anomalies, 0.5 ppd, S Pole
docs.description:
The Diviner Lunar Radiometer Experiment onboard the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LRO) has been acquiring solar reflectance and mid-infrared radiance measurements nearly continuously since July of 2009. Approximately a quarter trillion calibrated radiance measurements of the Moon, acquired over the first 5.5 years of the mission, have been compiled into our Level 4 - Global Cumulative Products (GCP). This data represents a compilation of all Diviner nadir observations from 5-July-2009 to 1-April-2015. They are produced by binning Diviner RDR (Level 1b) radiance measurements for each IR channel (channels 3-9) in 0.5 degree bins in longitude and latitude, and 0.25 hours of local time to determine the average brightness temperatures on a global cylindrical grid. Additionally, the average radiance values for all the channels were used to determine the bolometric brightness temperatures for each bin.

This map represents the maximum temperatures anomalies with zonal mean subtracted at 0.5 ppd. Maximum temperature variations are related to albedo. The average temperatures for given latitude subtracted out (zonal average removed) highlight anomalous temperatures due to variations in the regolith properties as well as the ratios and the difference between the minimum and maximum temperatures which highlight the relative differences between the two temperature extremes and the amplitude of the extremes in temperature. For more information, please refer to: Williams, J. P., Paige, D. A., Greenhagen, B. T., & Sefton-Nash, E. (2017). The global surface temperatures of the moon as measured by the Diviner Lunar Radiometer Experiment. Icarus, 283, 300-325.

docs.title: LRO DLRE Bolometric Brightness Temperature RGB Composite, 0.5 ppd, S Pole
docs.description:
The Diviner Lunar Radiometer Experiment onboard the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LRO) has been acquiring solar reflectance and mid-infrared radiance measurements nearly continuously since July of 2009. Approximately a quarter trillion calibrated radiance measurements of the Moon, acquired over the first 5.5 years of the mission, have been compiled into our Level 4 - Global Cumulative Products (GCP). This data represents a compilation of all Diviner nadir observations from 5-July-2009 to 1-April-2015. They are produced by binning Diviner RDR (Level 1b) radiance measurements for each IR channel (channels 3-9) in 0.5 degree bins in longitude and latitude, and 0.25 hours of local time to determine the average brightness temperatures on a global cylindrical grid. Additionally, the average radiance values for all the channels were used to determine the bolometric brightness temperatures for each bin.

This RGB composite map allows for broad characterization of terrains based on minimum and maximum temperatures (normalized by zonal mean temperatures). Maximum temperatures are sensitive to the radiative properties of the surface and minimum temperatures are sensitive to the thermophysical properties of the regolith. This characterization is highlighted in an RGB composite map (±70° latitude) where the red channel is visual brightness derived from Diviner’s visible channel (channel 1), the green channel is the minimum temperaures, and the blue channel is the maximum temperatures. Terrains can be characterized as low/high reflectance and low/high thermal inertia (TI). Young craters and rays (yellow/orange) are bright and high TI. Cold spots and radar dark halos (magenta) are bright and low TI, mare (cyan/blue) are dark and high TI, pyroclastic deposits (blue) are dark and low TI. For more information, please refer to: Williams, J. P., Paige, D. A., Greenhagen, B. T., & Sefton-Nash, E. (2017). The global surface temperatures of the moon as measured by the Diviner Lunar Radiometer Experiment. Icarus, 283, 300-325.

docs.title: GRAIL LGRS, Crust-mantle Interface Depth Model 1
docs.description: High-resolution gravity data obtained from the dual Gravity Recovery and Interior Laboratory (GRAIL) spacecraft show that the bulk density of the Moon’s highlands crust is 2550 kilograms per cubic meter, substantially lower than generally assumed. When combined with remote sensing and sample data, this density implies an average crustal porosity of 12% to depths of at least a few kilometers. Lateral variations in crustal porosity correlate with the largest impact basins, whereas lateral variations in crustal density correlate with crustal composition. The low-bulk crustal density allows construction of a global crustal thickness model that satisfies the Apollo seismic constraints, and with an average crustal thickness between 34 and 43 kilometers, the bulk refractory element composition of the Moon is not required to be enriched with respect to that of Earth.

docs.title: LP NS Water Equivalent Hydrogen SP
docs.description: This map of Water Equivalent Hydrogen is based  on an updated analysis of Lunar Prospector epithermal neutron data. An improved map of the distribution of hydrogen near to the lunar poles was achieved using a specially developed pixon image reconstruction algorithm to deconvolve the instrumental response of the Lunar Prospector's neutron spectrometer from the observed data, while simultaneously suppressing the statistical noise.
